base: Brief says v299; current main is v300 (d2c96eaf, Claude R124 lazy commit + descriptor pricing + docs). No v299 -> v300 drift for WS1/WS2: all seven WS1 probes identical on v299 (a4cc6540) and v300 (d2c96eaf), verified via worktrees at both versions.
follow_ups: The tracking fix must be flow-sensitive MUST-tracking (current type at each use site) OR refuse reassignment to a different type at compile time (type error, not segfault) OR use a runtime tag (contradicting the proposal's 'No runtime tag'). May-tracking (what was EVER assigned) is proven to crash on kosh -> raw reassignment and on control-flow-dependent reassignment (yadi c=1).

Mala descriptor, if pursued, should be justified by bounds-checking (mala currently has none, direct or via vitti) and uniformity, not by aliasing (no mala alias cliff exists: fixed-size, persistent, never moves, never freed).

Decision #3 (restrict nirmmita to its mandapa region) is incomplete without a rule for lib-function allocations: mandapa scratch is lexical, not dynamic - lib functions (mala_nava) called from inside a mandapa still allocate persistent and escape the block's rewind/budget (R124 WS1(c) bypass, confirmed for mala_nava).

Anyatha/else syntax was not resolved (zero usage in examples/lib); the control-flow case was proven with a single yadi instead, which suffices. If the language has no else, that should be documented; if it has one with different syntax, the branch test should be redone with it.
not_run: Windows execution (v300 lazy commit is Windows/PE and does not affect these Linux results - verified by identical WS1 results on v299 and v300)
implementation (test and analysis only, designs not built)
full suite (no tree changes; v300 suite numbers stand)

ws1.anyatha_limitation: Anyatha blocks do not parse in the form used (likha-only anyatha fails at the closing brace; assignment anyatha fails at '='); zero anyatha usage in examples/ or lib/. Language may have no else, or a different else syntax. Control-flow case proven instead with a single yadi (below), which suffices.
ws1.control_flow_yadi_c0: a = k initially; yadi (c=0) { a = p } does not execute; a[0] prints 11, exit 0 (correct, kosh code works on kosh buffer)
ws1.control_flow_yadi_c1: a = k initially; yadi (c=1) { a = p } executes, a becomes raw; a[0] segfaults exit 139 (may-analysis emits kosh code unconditionally, which crashes on a raw pointer; type is control-flow-dependent and not tracked)
ws1.direct_kosh_oob: k[100] on a 4-element kosh (2 pushed) refuses 'Sutram truti: mala ank seema atikram', exit 1, on both v299 and v300 - direct kosh indexing DOES bounds-check
ws1.direct_mala_oob: m[100] on a 4-element mala (2 filled) prints 0, exit 0, on both versions - mala NEVER bounds-checks, direct or via vitti
ws1.reassign_forward_kosh_to_raw: a = k (k[0]=11); a[0] prints 11; then a = p (p[0]=77); a[0] segfaults exit 139 (instead of 77), on both v299 and v300 - tracking is MAY-analysis (once ever assigned a kosh, always emit kosh code), not flow-sensitive MUST-analysis
ws1.reassign_reverse_raw_to_kosh: a = p (p[0]=77); a[0] prints 77; then a = k; a[0] prints 11; then a[100] refuses (bounds check), on both versions - raw -> kosh updates correctly (kosh code on a kosh buffer is correct); tracking is ASYMMETRIC
ws1.v299_vs_v300: All seven WS1 probes identical on v299 (a4cc6540) and v300 (d2c96eaf). The tracking (for kosh) and the reassignment segfault predate v300; they are NOT introduced by Claude's R124. Claude's R124 addendum ('vitti a = k is tracked') is consistent with pre-existing behaviour on both versions.
ws1.verdict: PARTLY FALSE, PARTLY TRUE, and the true part is worse than claimed. FALSE: 'compiler cannot tell which' - for straight-line kosh assignments it CAN tell (bounds-checked kosh code, distinct from unchecked raw/mala code). TRUE: for mala vs raw it CANNOT tell (both unchecked, identical behaviour). WORSE: for reassignment and control flow its tracking is MAY-analysis, so it crashes (segfault, not a clean error, not correct behaviour) instead of updating correctly or refusing. Proposal's 'statically track what was assigned' is ambiguous: may-tracking (EVER assigned) is proven wrong (crashes); flow-sensitive must-tracking (CURRENTLY assigned at each use site) is correct but harder, especially for branches/loops where the type is control-flow-dependent (must join/refuse/tag or duplicate code). Proposal as stated is INCOMPLETE: it does not address reassignment or control-flow-dependent types.
ws1.vitti_kosh_oob: vitti a = k; a[100] refuses, same error, exit 1, on both versions - vitti-held kosh DOES bounds-check (compiler tracks straight-line kosh assignment)
ws1.vitti_mala_oob: vitti a = m (mala 4 elements); a[100] prints 0, exit 0, on both versions - vitti-held mala does NOT bounds-check
ws1.vitti_nirm_oob: vitti a = p (nirmmita 16 bytes); a[100] prints 0, exit 0, on both versions - vitti-held raw pointer does NOT bounds-check

ws2.descriptor_for_mala_justification: UNNECESSARY for aliasing (no mala alias cliff exists: fixed-size, persistent, never moves, never freed, so aliases never break); USEFUL for bounds-checking (mala currently has none, direct or via vitti) and uniformity (one mechanism - a design choice, not a fix). Decision #2's justification ('alias cliff closes for both') is wrong for mala.
ws2.escape_check_contrast: Direct nirmmita inside a mandapa, assigned to outer vitti: REFUSED at compile time (E_SCRATCH_ESCAPE). Mala (via mala_nava, a lib function) inside a mandapa, assigned to outer vitti: ALLOWED (no refusal) - escape check does not track lib-function returns. Bypass is HARMLESS for lifetime because mala is persistent (never reclaimed), but it is a blind spot that would matter for a lib function allocating scratch.
ws2.mala_allocation: ARENA, not stack (mala_nava uses nirmmita, arena bump). PERSISTENT, lexically not dynamically: mala_nava defined outside any mandapa (lib/mala.smlib), so its internal nirmmita is lexically outside a mandapa -> persistent even when called from inside a mandapa. Evidence: two malas in two separate mandapa blocks at different addresses (123571923845120 vs 123571923845152, difference exactly 32 bytes = one 4-element mala buffer) - sequential persistent allocation, not scratch reuse (scratch would reuse the same address, difference 0). Reuse probe (second block writes 99, read first block's mala) still prints 41, confirming no reuse.
ws2.mala_returned_from_prakriya: Prints 41, survives (control, persistent, no mandapa). Mala created inside a mandapa, assigned to outer vitti, read after block: prints 41, survives (NOT refused, NOT garbage) - because it is persistent (lexical), it legitimately survives block exit (not dangling).
ws2.verdict: Answer's CONCLUSION (mala's alias is safe) is TRUE for lifetime, and safe BEYOND the block close (persistent, lexical, fixed-size, never freed) - not just until it. Its REASONING is incomplete: cites 'never moves' but omits 'never freed' (persistence, lexical not dynamic) and 'fixed size' (no growth, so no relocation - unlike kosh, which grows and relocates at MAXCAP). 'Never moves' alone does not guarantee safety. Decision #3 (restrict nirmmita to its mandapa region) is incomplete without a rule for lib-function allocations (lexical vs dynamic; R124 WS1(c) bypass, confirmed for mala_nava).

ws3.dependent_chain_10m: 0.054 s (5.4 ns/step), correct sum 5114877760, today on v300. Descriptor adds +2.240 ns/step (R125 hot dependent extra) x 10M = +22.4 ms -> ~0.076 s (+41%, 54 ms -> 76 ms).
ws3.descriptor_adds: Sequential loop: ~0 (R125 array-loop difference ~0, pipelined/hoisted, throughput-bound). Dependent loop: +22.4 ms for 10M steps (R125 hot dependent extra).
ws3.premise_correction: Brief's premise ('if a descriptor adds 2.2 ns to it, what does that cost in a tight loop?') assumes 2.2 ns per iteration applies to a tight (sequential) loop - WRONG. 2.2 ns is a LATENCY (dependent chain) cost, not a THROUGHPUT (sequential loop) cost. Mala's 'fast' reputation for sequential loops is NOT threatened by descriptors (free there); for pointer-chasing loops the cost is real (+41% for 10M steps) but not catastrophic (54 ms -> 76 ms).
ws3.sequential_10m: 0.074 s (7.4 ns/iter), correct sum 5114877120, today on v300 (mala 1024 elements, wrapping counter, no division). Descriptor sequential total ~0.074 s (no measurable increase).
ws3.sequential_division_caution: An earlier sequential loop using division for modulo (j - (j/1024)*1024) took 0.328 s (32.8 ns/iter), dominated by integer division (25.4 ns/division), not by mala access. Wrapping-counter version (0.074 s) is the clean measurement; both print the same correct sum, confirming the difference is division overhead, not mala access.
